approach.title: Iterative relinking down the left spine
approach.explanation: Walk down the left spine from the root. For each node, remember its left child as the next node, then set its left to the previous node's right child and its right to the previous node. Keep the current node's old right child for the next step. When the walk ends, the last node is the new root.
chooseWhen: The transformation follows only the left spine.
Constant extra memory is possible.
tradeoffs: A recursive version is shorter but uses O(h) stack.
Building a fresh tree costs more memory than relinking.
invariants: prev is the root of the already flipped upper part; prev_right is the old right child of prev.
hints: Which nodes move?
Only nodes on the left spine; right children are leaves that become left children.
Iterate with three pointers: current, previous and previous right.

stages.title: Trace the flip
stages.question: What happens to one parent and its two children?
stages.explanation: The left child becomes the parent; the old right child becomes its left child; the old parent becomes its right child.
stages.rationale: Repeating this along the left spine flips the whole tree.
observations: The leftmost leaf becomes the root.
hints: Follow only the left spine.

stages.title: Implement iteratively
stages.question: How do you avoid losing pointers?
stages.explanation: Save next = cur.left before overwriting, then set cur.left = prev_right, save prev_right = cur.right, set cur.right = prev, and advance.
stages.rationale: The order of assignments matters.
instructions: Serialise the new root back to a level-order list without trailing None.
observations: The original root ends as a leaf with both children None.
hints: Save cur.right before overwriting it.

approach.title: Sprague-Grundy values per run of '+'
approach.explanation: Each maximal run of '+' is an independent game. Flipping two characters inside a run of length L splits it into runs of lengths i and L - 2 - i. The Grundy value g(L) is the smallest non-negative integer not among g(i) xor g(L-2-i). The whole position is winning exactly when the xor of g over all runs is non-zero.
chooseWhen: The game splits into independent subgames.
Plain memoised search over strings is exponential.
tradeoffs: Backtracking with memoisation on the string works for short inputs but is much slower.
Grundy theory requires normal play (last mover wins), which holds here.
invariants: g[L] is the Grundy value of a run of length L.
The xor of the run values decides the winner.
hints: Do separate runs of '+' affect each other?
No; they are independent games.
Compute Grundy numbers for run lengths and xor them.
